::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives

- Replace a sample name in a rule with a `{sample}` wildcard.
- Explain how Snakemake works out a wildcard's value from the file it needs.
- Write `rule all` with `expand()` so that `snakemake` alone builds everything.
- Read a dry run's job stats and predict them before you run.
- Recognize an ambiguous pattern and fix it with `wildcard_constraints`.

Time: 45 min
:::

## From one sample to ten

The module 1 `fastqc` rule has `HCT116_CTCF_1` written into it three times.
Replace the name with `{sample}`:

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
rule fastqc:
    input:
        "../../data/fastq/{sample}.fastq.gz",
    output:
        html = "output/{sample}/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.html",
        zip = "output/{sample}/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.zip",
    shell:
        "fastqc --outdir output/{wildcards.sample}/fastqc {input}"
```

`{sample}` in `input:` and `output:` is a **wildcard**: it stands for any
text. The rule is now a pattern that can make FastQC reports for any sample
whose FASTQ exists.

In `shell:` the wildcard is `{wildcards.sample}`, not `{sample}`. Inside the
command, the names you can use are `input`, `output`, `wildcards`, `threads`,
`params`, `log` and global Python variables. Exercise 2.4 shows the error you
get otherwise.

## How Snakemake fills in a wildcard

Ask for a file:

```bash
snakemake -n output/HCT116_CTCF_2/fastqc/HCT116_CTCF_2_fastqc.html
```

1. Snakemake looks for a rule with an output pattern that matches the name.
   `output/{sample}/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.html` matches with
   `sample=HCT116_CTCF_2`. A wildcard used twice must match the same text both
   times.
2. It fills the same value into `input:`:
   `../../data/fastq/HCT116_CTCF_2.fastq.gz`.
3. If that file exists, or another rule can make it, the job is planned.

Wildcards always flow from outputs to inputs. Snakemake never looks in
`data/fastq/` to see which samples exist. It only knows what you ask for.

::: {.notes}
This is the moment to say it twice: Snakemake works backward. The FASTQ folder
could hold a hundred files; if nothing asks for their outputs, nothing runs.
:::

## No target, no sample

Now run `snakemake -n` with no target. If `fastqc` is the first rule:

<!-- GENERATE: lesson02-no-target | stopping-points/stopA | cat > Snakefile <<'EOF'

snakemake -n || true -->

{{< generated name="lesson02-no-target" command="false" >}}

The default target is the first rule's output, and that output has a
wildcard nobody filled in. The message already names the fix: a rule without
wildcards at the top that lists every file you want.

## `rule all` and `expand()`

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
SAMPLES = ["HCT116_CTCF_1", "HCT116_CTCF_2"]

rule all:
    input:
        expand("output/{sample}/fastqc/{sample}_fastqc.html", sample=SAMPLES),
```

`rule all` has only inputs. It makes nothing itself; it exists so that its
inputs become the targets. `expand()` fills a pattern once per value:

```python
>>> expand("output/{sample}/{sample}_filtered.bam", sample=["HCT116_CTCF_1", "HCT116_CTCF_2"])
['output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered.bam', 'output/HCT116_CTCF_2/HCT116_CTCF_2_filtered.bam']
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`expand()` is ordinary Python that runs when the Snakefile is read, so the
list is fixed before Snakemake plans anything. It is not a wildcard. With two
lists (`expand("{a}_{b}", a=[...], b=[...])`) you get every combination.
:::

## Paths in one place

The paths `../../data` and `output` now appear in every rule. Put them in
variables, as stopping point A does:

{{< snippet repo="stopA" file="Snakefile" lines="9-28" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`DATA + "/fastq/{sample}.fastq.gz"` is plain string concatenation: the result
still contains `{sample}`, which Snakemake treats as a wildcard. In `shell:`,
`{OUT}` is a global variable and is filled in like `{input}`. The sample list
and the MAPQ settings are still in the Snakefile. Module 3 moves them to a
samplesheet and a config file.
:::

## Every sample through `align`

{{< snippet repo="stopA" file="Snakefile" rule="align" >}}

The module 1 rule with `HCT116_CTCF_1` replaced by `{sample}`. The index has
no wildcard, so every `align` job depends on the same one `bowtie2_index` job.

## And through `filter`

{{< snippet repo="stopA" file="Snakefile" rule="filter" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The input of `filter` is the output pattern of `align`. When `rule all` asks
for `output/HCT116_DNase_1/HCT116_DNase_1_filtered.bam`, Snakemake fills in
`sample=HCT116_DNase_1` here, needs `output/HCT116_DNase_1/HCT116_DNase_1_aligned.bam`,
finds that `align` can make it, and so on back to the FASTQ. The 20 files in
`rule all` become 31 jobs, plus `rule all` itself.

The shell block is four commands. `{MIN_MAPQ}` and `{EXCLUDE_FLAGS}` are
global variables. 1804 is the ENCODE ChIP-seq filter: unmapped, mate unmapped,
secondary, QC fail and duplicate.
:::

## When a name does not match

Wildcards match text, so a typo in a target does not mean "file not found".
It means no rule has an output pattern that fits:

```bash
snakemake -n output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1.bam
```

<!-- GENERATE: stopA-no-rule | stopping-points/stopA | snakemake -n output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1.bam || true -->

{{< generated name="stopA-no-rule" >}}

`filter` makes `..._filtered.bam` and `align` makes `..._aligned.bam`. Nothing
makes a plain `{sample}.bam`.

## Constraining wildcards

A wildcard matches any text, slashes included. Usually that is harmless. It
becomes a problem when two rules could make the same file, or when one pattern
can split a name in more than one place. The fix is to say what a wildcard is
allowed to be. MicroCPipe restricts its two wildcards to the names in the
samplesheet:

{{< snippet repo="microcpipe" file="workflows/MicroCPipe.snakefile" lines="33-35" >}}

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`"|".join(...)` builds a regular expression such as
`GM12878_ctrl_1|GM12878_ctrl_2`, so `{group}` can only be one of those names.
`re.escape` protects characters that mean something in a regular expression,
like the `.` in a name such as `GM12878.ctrl`. With the constraint, a typo in
a target fails with "No rule to produce" right away. Stopping point B adds the
same block for `{sample}` (module 3). Exercise 2.2 shows the error a missing
constraint causes.
:::

## Exercise 2.2: Make it ambiguous, then fix it

In your copy of stopping point A, add a general rule that indexes any BAM:

```{.python filename="Snakefile"}
rule index_bam:
    input:
        "{prefix}.bam",
    output:
        "{prefix}.bam.bai",
    shell:
        "samtools index {input}"
```

Run `snakemake -n output/HCT116_CTCF_1/HCT116_CTCF_1_filtered.bam.bai`. Read
the error. Then fix it with `wildcard_constraints`, without deleting the new
rule.

## Stopping point A

::: {.callout-important .stopping-point}
## Stopping point A

`stopping-points/stopA/Snakefile` is the state of the pipeline now: FastQC,
the bowtie2 index, alignment and filtering for all ten samples, with
`{sample}` wildcards and `expand()`. A dry run plans 32 jobs; a full run takes
about 46 s on a 4-core laptop.

If your own Snakefile does not run, copy this one and carry on from there:

```bash
cp -r stopping-points/stopA work/regpipe-A
cd work/regpipe-A
snakemake -n
snakemake --cores 4
```
:::

## Key points

- `{sample}` in an output makes a rule a pattern. Snakemake fills in the
  value by matching the file it needs, then uses the same value in the inputs.
- In `shell:`, write `{wildcards.sample}`.
- `rule all` comes first and lists the final files; `expand()` builds that
  list from your sample names.
- Wildcards flow backward from targets. Snakemake never scans folders to find
  samples.
- When two rules can make the same file, or a pattern is too loose, constrain
  the wildcard.
